physical_harm: Fatal injuries caused by a chopper to the neck resulting in death
premeditation_planning: The court found no premeditation or planning, as the appellant acted callously and without hesitation
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular evidence corroborated by medical evidence, including the blood-stained chopper found with the appellant and the post-mortem report indicating the injuries were caused by a weapon similar to the one seized from the appellant.
witness_credibility: PW1 and PW5 clearly stated how the appellant had approached them with a blood-stained chopper and his 8-month-old son, and their accounts were corroborated by medical evidence. The evidence given by DW1 was rightly discarded by the High Court.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant made up his mind to ensure that the child be put into proper care and custody after the murder, and his conduct before and after the incident was sufficient to negate any notion that he was mentally insane.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant assaulted his wife with a chopper on her neck, resulting in her death. The evidence, including ocular and medical testimony, corroborated the act, and the appellant's conduct before and after the incident indicated his awareness of the nature of his actions.
defence_argument: The defence claimed the appellant suffered from paranoid schizophrenia and that his cognitive faculties were impaired at the time of the crime, making him incapable of knowing the nature of his act. They argued that the medical evidence supported this claim.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the accused must prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that at the time of the crime, he was incapable of knowing the nature of his act or that it was wrong or contrary to law, as per Section 84 of the Indian Penal Code.
precedent_relied_upon: R. vs. Daniel Me Naughten 1843 RR 59: 8ER 718(HL); Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar vs. State of Gujarat AIR 1964 SC 1563; Ratan Lal vs. State of Madhya Pradesh 1970 (3) sec 533
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the courts concluded that the appellant was fully aware of the nature of his act and its consequences, and there was no evidence to support his claim of insanity at the time of the crime.
